$comment: Shared client-in-the-loop e2e fixtures. Read verbatim by the TypeScript, Dart
and Rust suites so all three assert against IDENTICAL inputs and IDENTICAL
expectations. Never edit a payload without re-deriving every `expected` value
from the syncer.c v0.2.0 merge policy that BOTH the server and the clients use:
arrayStrategy      = MERGE_BY_KEY (4)
arrayMatchKeys     = "id"
resolveByTimestamp = true
lwwKeys            = "updatedAt,syncedAt"
fwwKeys            = (unset)
Policy facts these fixtures depend on (see syncer.c core/src/syncer.c):
* Rejection is WHOLE-OBJECT and per level: if base has a strictly newer
lwwKey than incoming, the entire incoming object at that level is dropped
(keys present only in incoming are NOT copied).
* A guard only applies when BOTH sides carry the key. An object with no
updatedAt on either side is a plain last-writer-wins deep merge, so for
unguarded scalars the ARRIVAL ORDER decides. Fixtures exploit both.
* fwwKeys: an incoming object whose createdAt is NEWER than base's is
rejected wholesale. Client payloads therefore omit createdAt for objects
that already exist on the server.
* MERGE_BY_KEY appends unmatched identities at the END of the base array, so
array order in `expected` is significant and deterministic.
* Array elements with no identity key (e.g. strings) get UNION semantics,
which is what makes replaying a queue idempotent.
No payload carries a top-level "id": the document id lives in the URL, so
these payloads need no per-language templating.

offlineQueue.$doc: Scenario 1 - queue 3 mutations offline, then flush. Run twice: once one-by-one via POST /doc/:id/sync, once atomically via POST /sync/batch. Both must land on the same `expected`.

optimisticPullback.$doc: Scenario 2 - apply a mutation locally through the client's reconcile path, push it, pull the server doc back, reconcile it into the local copy. Local and server must agree semantically (deep-equal after parse; jsonb reorders keys so raw strings are never compared).

staleRejection.$doc: Scenario 3 - both directions of timestamp resolution, round-tripped through the server. First the server holds an OLDER state: pulling it into the newer local copy must change nothing at all (whole-object rejection, so sOnly is not even copied). Then the server holds a NEWER state: it wins, and this time the merge descends, so the local-only key survives alongside the server's keys.

keyedArray.$doc: Scenario 4 - keyed-array reconciliation through the full stack. r1 is untouched by the client and must survive; r2 is updated with a FRESHER updatedAt and must be applied; r3 is updated with a STALER updatedAt and must be rejected wholesale; r4 is new and must be appended at the end.

replayIdempotency.$doc: Scenario 5 - flush the SAME queued mutation twice, as a client would after an ambiguous network failure. The document version must advance (proving the second write really executed) while the data stays byte-for-byte semantically identical. `tags` covers the identity-less array path, whose UNION semantics is what keeps replay from duplicating elements.

failureMarking.$doc: Scenario 6 - a mutation aimed at a document that does not exist must come back 404 and be marked FAILED, never SYNCED. The doc suffix `missingSuffix` is deliberately never created. A second mutation against a real document then proves the store's pending/synced/failed accounting is per-mutation and not sticky.
